newsitem.title: USA: Dole takes campaign to jail.
newsitem.headline: Dole takes campaign to jail.

text.p: Republican presidential candidate Bob Dole took his campaign to a jail on Tuesday in the company of "America's toughest sheriff" as he tried to lock up votes with his new anti-crime programme.

Dole toured a "get-tough" prison where inmates are housed in tents in the desert under the auspices of Maricopa County Sheriff Joe Arpaio, described by the Dole campaign as "internationally known as America's toughest sheriff."

At a forum for crime victims, held on the jail grounds, Dole repeated his call for harsher punishments for criminals and tougher anti-drug measures. "We're going to end the revolving door of justice," he said.
Arpaio endorsed Dole, giving him some law enforcement support he was denied on Monday when the 270,000-member Fraternal Order of Police endorsed Democratic President Bill Clinton.
"We need a president who will get tough on drug enforcement and he (Dole) is the one who will get tough," Arpaio said.
Said Dole, "The president got the leadership of the FOP. I'll get about 80 percent of the men and women who are walking the beat and doing the work every day, every day and every day."
At the Estrella Jail Facility, Arpaio has banned coffee, pornographic magazines, smoking and long hair, feeds imates cold bologna sandwiches and believes in chain gangs as a form of rehabilitation.

The stop was part of an anti-crime push by Dole, who put his tax-cutting economic programme on the back burner this week. Dole outlined a crime and drug policy proposal on Monday in a speech at Villanova University near Philadelphia.
In Phoenix, Dole cited Arpaio's low-budget tent solution to prison space and the work requirements. "We're going to make prisoners work. They work here," Dole said.
"This is not a country club. This is one of the points in my five-point programme," he said.
Dole then paid a short visit to former Arizona Sen. Barry Goldwater, patriarch of the modern conservative movement and the unsuccessful 1964 Republican presidential nominee.

Goldwater, 87, entered a hospital last Tuesday with a mild stroke and is currently undergoing physical and speech therapy. Dole met him on a hospital patio, where Goldwater, wearing a green golf shirt, and his wife, Susan, chatted briefly.

"(I) put on my Barry Goldwater button -- '64 -- he set on his Dole-Kemp sticker. He's doing very well, according to his doctors. Looks good, feels good," Dole said after the meeting, wearing the button which read "Goldwater in 64."
"Probably get to go home pretty soon," he said.
Arizona, with eight electoral votes out of the 270 needed to win, is usually safe Republican territory -- it has not backed a Democratic presidential candidate since Harry Truman in 1948.
But an Arizona State University poll taken in late August showed Clinton with a seven-point lead over Dole, at 43-36 percent. Ross Perot trailed with six percent.

The Arizona Republic newspaper, however, reported on Tuesday that an internal Dole campaign poll taken in late August showed Dole leading 41 percent to 40 percent in the state, with nine percent supporting Perot.
Dole said after meeting with Goldwater that he remained confident, and was encouraged by some national polls showing the race narrowing.
"Now we're down to single digits again. I don't know what the press is going to write about it, but it (the poll gap) is closing and we've got some debates coming up."
He said earlier of the debates, "I'm prepared. We're ready to go."
